stories.title_en: My monitor was cutting my download speed by 75%

comments.author: senko
comments.text:
This reminds me of a (completely different, but felt equally) bizzare problem with ghostty (the terminal emulator) on Linux and Steam, specifically Baldur's Gate 3.
At the start of the game after an update, BG3 compiles the (Vulkan) shaders. To avoid hammering the computer, it checks the load, including I/O pressure, and then throttles itself. It turns out that Ghostty uses io_uring, and even if it's not doing anything this somehow counts as pressure. This was made worse by the fact that I usually have a dozen or so Ghostty windows.
End result, BG3 compiles shaders using 1 core, throttled, instead of all available 20 cores. Instead of a minute or so, it'd take several hours.
(For closure: I configured ghostty to use epoll instead. Probably not optimal but works around the problem.)

comments.author: fancyfredbot
comments.text:
Since lots of comments misunderstood the article, the extra latency from going through the monitor meant his laptop couldn't acknowledge the packets quickly enough. That led a buffer on the ethernet adapter to fill and that led it to drop packets.
A different adapter which required less frequent acknowledgement fixed the problem for him.
It is quite a nice post which gets to the bottom of incredibly opaque behaviour of USB hubs.

comments.author: nagisa
comments.text:
I recently had this same problem with a multigig copper SFP+ module. These SFP+ modules (usually) advertise 10Gbps to the NIC they're plugged in, but will negotiate lower speeds on the copper side. So when NIC tries to send to SFP+ at higher rate than whatever speed SFP+ has negotiated internally, the SFP+ module will just drop a bunch of packets and incur a significant hit in throughput.
These tend to not support sending pause frames to its SFP+ side either, so the best option I found was to set bandwidth limit on the NIC…

I have nothing useful to add other than I feel so validated reading this. Ive been struggling with this issue on and off for over a year. With the release of Astra, it was able to finally unstick me to the point of enabling flow control which has been good enough.
I experienced this problem with a macbook and a thunderbolt dock. I had tried multiple different brands of docks and ethernet adapters, and various macbooks. One interesting thing I discovered is if I plugged a non-thunderbolt cable between the dock and the laptop, I would achieve full speed with no packet loss, so interestingly the issue doesn't occur over pure USB but only over thunderbolt.
This has got to be a bug on Apple's side right? Would be nice if they fixed it.

comments.author: frizkie
comments.text:
I had the same problem recently when trying to figure out high bandwidth game streaming from my desktop to my Steam deck in the living room. The beta streaming tech is “pyrowave” and it is super low latency and looks INCREDIBLE compared to traditional codecs, but as a trade off it is extremely sensitive to packet loss, and uses an appropriately large amount of bandwidth (7-800mbit at 4k120). Wired network isn’t _strictly_ a requirement but it might as well be, and the steam deck doesn’t have a physical port - but the steam deck dock does.
Anyway, the exact same situation arises, where some network condition or physical configuration (there’s a lot of hardware in between these two devices, including MoCA adapters) meant that the network adapter buffer fills up and starts dropping packets. The buffer size is configurable through some terminal command and maxing that out makes the issue disappear immediately.

comments.author: dawdler-purge
comments.text:
I was  when saw this in the morning. I thought I could no longer be surprised by AI progress. Yet I had not truly believed that Claude could prove a conjecture as challenging as the Riemann Hypothesis.
In fact, just this summer, I tried to write a short science fiction story, The Last Conjecture, about AI working on the Riemann Hypothesis — a bad, unpublished story that I wrote with the help of AI itself. The irony is that even the AI helping me write it could not believe that AI would solve the Riemann Hypothesis in any near future. In its own forecast for the story, the project drags on for nine years, all the way to 2035, and still never cracks it.
Just yesterday, on Friday, I was still telling students: “Maybe there is some physical law that limits how much intelligence one can get from current LLM architectures. Surely nothing in this universe is infinite.” Maybe I am right. It is just that on November 21, 2026, we have not yet reached that limit.
It was 7 a.m. I opened the curtains in my study. The sun was rising. It was a sunny day. Nothing had changed. Everything had changed.
Seeking some solace, I listened to a recent episode of the 3Blue1Brown podcast with host Grant Sand

comments.author: spprashant

I am hopeful we will see cheap abundant nutritious food and clean water, more efficient solar batteries, economical space travel, cancer treatments, climate change mitigation etc. Most importantly, I hope people can still find purpose in their lifespans. Maybe a few centuries from now it would be thought of as barbaric that people we forced to sit on a desk for 8 hours a day just to afford a livelihood.

comments.author: vbezhenar
comments.text:
What I found surprising. How many absolutely groundbreaking breakthroughs with AI are in Mathematics. And at the same time I can't remember anything similar in other fields. For example there's nothing groundbreaking in Software. Yes, Claude can write some PoC code faster than me. Great. What about creating some software which wasn't possible before? What about creating operating system without a single bug? What about inventing some video compression which is miles ahead of competitors? What about creating Rust compiler which runs 10x faster than rustc?
I think the closest thing is formal verification of Signal protocol, I guess. Which is insanely cool, but still not as cool as millenium problem.

comments.author: Fredkin
comments.text:
I really hope Levent next tries to prove the irrationality of the Euler-Mascheroni constant ɣ , or the gamma function minimum α, Γ(α) , as they have so many forms yet we know so little about them. It's slightly related to GRH, since the Zeta function occurs in a some of these forms.
